en: Your phone says debited. The shop says nothing came. So where is your eight hundred and forty rupees right now?
It isn't lost. It's sitting in one bank's account. I'll show you which one, when it comes back, and the one mistake that makes you pay twice.
Let me tell you the secret. U.P.I. runs on two layers. The first layer only moves messages, and every bank gets fifteen seconds to reply.
The second layer moves the actual money, later, in batches. Ten times a day, banks settle up through their accounts at the R.B.I.
So the word your app shows is only about the messages. Makes sense?
Success means both banks replied. Failed means it broke early — your money never left, or your bank sends it back. Failed is safe to try again.
Now the big one... processing.
Your bank replied, done. But the shop's bank went silent.
After fifteen seconds, N.P.C.I. stops waiting, and here's the catch — it marks your payment deemed approved. Approved for now, checked later.
So in the next money batch, your eight hundred and forty rupees really moves to the shop's bank. That's where your money is right now.
The next day, the shop's bank checks its books and must file one of two answers.
Answer one, T.C.C. — we credited the shop. The shop has your money, even though its speaker stayed silent.
Answer two, R.E.T. — return. The shop never got it, so the money goes back, and your bank puts it in your account.
That's why refunds come the next day, not in seconds.
And the R.B.I. sets a deadline. Sent to a person? Back by the next day. Paid a shop? Within five days.
Miss it — and the bank pays you one hundred rupees for every extra day. You don't even have to ask.
So what should you do at the counter? Here's what I do.
First, never pay again while it says processing. If the answer is T.C.C. — you've paid twice.
Second, ask the shopkeeper to check their bank statement, not the speaker.
Third, if nothing comes back by the deadline, complain in your app's U.P.I. Help, and then to your bank.
Cleared your doubt? Send this to that friend who always pays twice.
That's the payment that breaks. But what happens when a payment goes right? Watch this next one.
